title: Refrigerated transport
description: Lets meat, fruit and milk cross oceans without spoiling, which is why shops sell food from the other side of the world. A machine on board squeezes air, cools it with seawater, then lets it expand; air that expands gets very cold, and it is blown through an insulated hold kept below freezing.
draw: Cutaway of a late-1800s steamship's hold: an insulated room with thick walls, frosty carcasses of mutton hanging from hooks, and cold-air ducts along the ceiling leading from a steam-driven compressor engine in the next compartment. Show the outer hull and the sea outside so it is clearly a ship.
flag: 1880 is the Strathleven's frozen beef and mutton from Australia to London, chilled by a Bell-Coleman air machine (Glasgow). Rivals: Charles Tellier's Frigorifique (France, 1876-77), the Paraguay (1877), Swift's iced rail cars (US, 1878), and the Dunedin (NZ, 1882), which launched the trade. Overlaps Refrigerators (1858).

title: Tractor
description: Pulls ploughs, harvesters and trailers, doing the work of a team of horses without fields of oats to feed them. A petrol or diesel engine turns the big rear wheels through low gears that trade speed for pulling force, and deep treads dig into the soil so the wheels grip instead of spinning.
draw: An early farm tractor seen from the side, pulling a plough through a field: engine at the front, driver's seat over the rear axle, huge rear wheels with angled cleats or chevron treads biting into the soil, and small steerable front wheels. A drawbar links the back of the tractor to the plough, whose blades turn the soil over behind.
flag: 1892 is Froelich's petrol tractor, which threshed grain that season but sold poorly; Hart-Parr (1902) was the first commercial success and the Fordson (1917) the first mass-produced. Rubber tyres (in the hint) came only in 1932.

title: Air conditioning
description: Keeps buildings cool and dry in hot weather. A liquid refrigerant evaporates inside a coil indoors, soaking up heat from the air blown across it, while water from the air condenses on the cold fins; a compressor then squeezes the vapour so it gets hot and dumps that heat outdoors through a second coil.
draw: A cutaway window air conditioner set in a window frame: on the room side a fan blows air through a cold finned coil beaded with condensation; in the middle sits a round compressor; on the outdoor side a second fan pushes air through a hot finned coil. Copper tubes join the two coils and the compressor in one closed loop.
flag: Carrier's 1902 system in a Brooklyn printing plant was built to control humidity for the paper, not for comfort.

title: Washing machine
inventor: Alva J. Fisher, Hurley Machine Company
description: Washes a load of clothes without anyone scrubbing or wringing by hand. An electric motor turns a perforated drum, or a paddle in a tub, back and forth so soapy water is pushed through the cloth again and again; then the drum spins fast, flinging the water out through its holes.
draw: A front-loading washing machine with its round glass door shut and a cutaway side: a perforated steel drum turning on a horizontal axle, with raised ribs inside that lift the clothes and drop them into soapy water pooled at the bottom. A belt runs from an electric motor under the tub to a pulley on the back of the drum.
flag: Fisher's priority is disputed (a Binghamton firm claimed an electric washer in 1906); the Thor is usually cited as the first sold widely, from 1908.

title: Zipper
description: Closes a jacket, bag or tent in one pull. Each metal or plastic tooth has a bump on top and a hollow underneath; the Y-shaped slider bends the two rows apart and feeds them together at an angle, so each tooth nests between two teeth on the other side and the bumps lock into the hollows.
draw: Close-up of a metal zip half done up on a jacket, closed end at the bottom: below the slider the two rows of teeth are meshed in a single tight line; above it they spread apart in a V. The slider is a small Y-shaped channel with a wedge inside its wide top end that pushes the rows apart, and a pull tab hanging from its front.
flag: Whitcomb Judson's 'clasp locker' (1893) came first but jammed; Sundback's 1913 'Hookless No. 2' is the modern design.

title: Frozen food
description: Keeps food tasting fresh for months. Packed food is pressed between metal plates or belts chilled far below freezing, so it freezes solid in minutes rather than hours. Fast freezing forms ice crystals too small to burst the food's cells, so it is not mushy when thawed.
draw: Two long stainless-steel conveyor belts running one above the other, sandwiching a row of flat cardboard cartons of food between them; the belts are thick with frost, and icy brine sprays onto their outer faces from pipes above and below. At the far end the cartons come out frozen hard.
flag: 1924 is when Birdseye founded General Seafood to quick-freeze fish; frozen food first went on sale in shops in 1930 (Springfield, Massachusetts).

title: Fibreglass
inventor: Games Slayter and Dale Kleist, Owens-Illinois
description: Glass spun into strands finer than a hair. A loose wool of it traps air and insulates houses; strands set in plastic resin make light, strong boats, car bodies and wind-turbine blades. Molten glass runs through hundreds of tiny holes in a hot metal plate and is pulled out into threads so thin they bend instead of snapping.
draw: Underneath a glowing-hot metal box, hundreds of fine streams of molten glass drip from rows of tiny nozzles and are drawn down into shining filaments, which converge through a guide into a single strand that winds onto a fast-spinning drum below.
flag: Kleist made glass wool by accident in 1932 and Slayter developed the process (patented 1933); the 'Fiberglas' name dates from 1936-38, and glass-fibre plastics for boats from the 1940s.

title: Heat pump
description: Heats a building with a third or less of the electricity a heater would use. It is a refrigerator run backwards: a cold refrigerant evaporates in an outdoor coil, soaking up warmth even from chilly air, ground or river water; a compressor squeezes the vapour hot, and it gives that heat up indoors as it condenses.
draw: An outdoor heat-pump unit on short feet beside a house wall: a metal box with a large round fan grille on its front and thin aluminium fins along its back, lightly frosted. Two insulated copper pipes run from its side through the wall into the house.
flag: Year changed from 1940 to 1938: the heat pump in Zurich's town hall (1937-38, drawing heat from the river Limmat) is the first large working one. Peter von Rittinger built one for an Austrian salt works in 1856; Robert Webber's home ground-source pump was about 1948 (US). Overlaps Refrigerators and Air conditioning.

title: Randomized controlled trial
inventor: Austin Bradford Hill, Medical Research Council
description: A fair test of whether a treatment works. Patients are split into two groups purely by chance, for instance by sealed envelopes, and one group gets the treatment while the other does not. Chance spreads age, health and every hidden difference evenly, so any gap in how the groups fare is down to the treatment.
draw: On a hospital bedside table, a doctor's hand draws a card out of one of a stack of identical sealed envelopes; beside it stand two identical medicine bottles, one with a white cap and one with a blue cap, standing for the two groups. A hospital bed is softly visible behind.
flag: 1948 is the MRC streptomycin trial for tuberculosis. James Lind's 1747 scurvy test was controlled but not randomized.

title: Credit card
inventor: Frank McNamara and Ralph Schneider, Diners Club
description: Lets you buy now and pay later without carrying cash. The card names your account; the shop passes the charge to the card company, which pays the shop and sends you one bill a month. Later cards held the account number in a magnetic stripe, as tiny magnetised patches a reader senses, and now in a chip.
draw: A hand swiping a plain plastic card through the slot of a countertop card reader, the dark magnetic stripe on the back of the card facing into the slot where the reading head sits. No lettering or logos on the card or the reader.
flag: Diners Club (1950) was a cardboard charge card paid off monthly; BankAmericard (1958) was the first widely used revolving-credit card, and the magnetic stripe came from IBM in the 1960s.

title: Tunnel boring machine
description: Digs tunnels for railways, roads and water through solid rock. A wheel as wide as the tunnel, studded with hard steel cutters, turns while hydraulic rams press it into the rock face; rolling disc cutters crack off chips, a conveyor carries them back, and the machine braces against the walls to push itself forward.
draw: Three-quarter view inside a part-dug rock tunnel: the machine's round cutterhead fills the tunnel face, a flat steel disc studded with rows of small steel cutting wheels set in concentric rings, with slots between them for broken rock. Behind it a long trailing frame carries a conveyor belt heaped with rock back along the tunnel.
flag: Robbins's 1952 machine bored tunnels at the Oahe Dam, South Dakota; his rolling disc cutters came in 1956. Frederick Beaumont's compressed-air machine bored nearly 2 km of a trial Channel Tunnel in the early 1880s and could count as an earlier working one.

title: Nuclear submarine
description: A submarine that can stay underwater for months, not hours. In its reactor, splitting uranium heats water in a sealed loop; that water boils water in a second loop into steam, which spins a turbine to drive the propeller. Because nothing burns, it needs no air, and its time submerged is limited mainly by the crew's food.
draw: Cutaway side view of a long, rounded submarine underwater: a reactor in a thick shielded compartment amidships, steam pipes running aft to a turbine, and a single shaft from the turbine to one propeller at the stern. The sail (conning tower) rises from the top of the hull ahead of the reactor.
flag: USS Nautilus was commissioned in September 1954 but first got under way on nuclear power in January 1955. Overlaps Submarine (1898) and Controlled fission reactors (1954).

title: Disposable syringe
description: Gives injections with a needle used once and thrown away, so it cannot carry disease from one patient to the next. A rubber-tipped plunger seals against the wall of a clear plastic barrel: pulling it back lowers the pressure inside, and the outside air pressure pushes medicine up through the hollow steel needle.
draw: A clear plastic syringe with fine graduation lines (no numbers), its rubber-tipped plunger pulled halfway back, held upright beneath an upside-down glass vial; the steel needle pierces the vial's rubber stopper and liquid is rising into the barrel.
flag: First is disputed: Roehr Products (US) sold a plastic disposable syringe in 1955, Charles Rothauser (Australia) reportedly made one in 1949, Murdoch patented his in 1956, and Becton Dickinson's Plastipak (1961) made them common.

title: Spandex
description: A fibre that stretches to several times its length and springs back, used in sportswear, socks, waistbands and most stretch jeans. Its long molecules alternate soft, coiled, rubbery stretches with short stiff ones that stick to their neighbours; pulling uncoils the soft parts, and the stiff parts hold everything together so it snaps back.
draw: Two hands pulling a strip of shiny knitted stretch fabric to about twice its length, the knit loops visibly elongated in the stretched middle while the ends stay loose and gathered.
flag: Re Boris's note: a modest invention, but a few percent of it is in a large share of the world's clothing. Invented 1958; on sale (as Lycra, a brand) from about 1960-62.

title: Three-point seat belt
description: Holds you in your seat in a crash instead of letting you fly into the windscreen. One belt runs low across the hips and diagonally across the chest, anchored at three points, so the force lands on the strong pelvis and ribcage. A weighted catch in the reel locks the belt when the car brakes hard.
draw: A driver sitting in a car seat wearing a three-point belt: the lap part lies low across the hips, and the shoulder part runs diagonally from a mount on the door pillar above the outer shoulder, across the chest, down to a buckle beside the inner hip. The belt comes out of a reel low on the door pillar.
flag: The first 1959 Volvo belts were fixed; inertia-locking reels came a few years later.

title: Hip replacement
description: Replaces a hip joint worn out by arthritis, so people can walk again without pain. A polished steel ball on a stem is fixed into the hollow of the thigh bone with bone cement and turns inside a plastic cup cemented into the pelvis. The small ball and slippery plastic keep friction and wear low for decades.
draw: Cutaway of a human hip, front view: the pelvis with a white plastic cup set into its socket, and a polished metal ball sitting in that cup, mounted on a tapered metal stem pushed down into the hollow centre of the thigh bone. The ball points up and inward toward the pelvis.
flag: Title shortened from 'Artificial hip / joint replacement'. 1962 is Charnley's switch to polyethylene cups at Wrightington Hospital; his 1958-62 Teflon cups wore out.

title: Fax machine
description: Sends a copy of a page across the world over an ordinary phone line. The sending machine scans the page line by line, a light-sensitive cell turning each spot's lightness or darkness into an electrical tone; the receiving machine listens to the tones and prints matching dots, line by line, to rebuild the page.
draw: A desktop fax machine with a telephone handset resting on top, a sheet of paper being drawn face-down into its slot over a narrow bright strip of scanning light that shines across the full width of the page.
flag: Year changed from 1964 to 1966: Xerox's 1964 LDX needed special lines, while the 1966 Magnafax Telecopier (built with Magnavox) was the first to work over ordinary phone lines. Facsimile is far older: Caselli's pantelegraph ran a service in France in the 1860s, and newspapers sent wirephotos from the 1920s.

title: Night vision
description: Lets soldiers, rescuers and wildlife watchers see by starlight. A lens focuses the faint light onto a coated plate where each particle of light knocks out an electron; a high voltage speeds the electrons up and multiplies them thousands of times, and they strike a phosphor screen that glows green with a bright copy of the scene.
draw: A pair of night-vision goggles mounted on the front of a helmet and flipped down: two short tubes with objective lenses facing forward and eyepieces at the back, each eyepiece glowing faint green. Dark night background.
flag: Title changed from 'Night-vision goggles': the first starlight devices (Vietnam, mid-1960s; sources give 1964-67) were rifle scopes, and head-worn goggles followed in the 1970s. Germany's 1945 'Vampir' saw by an infrared lamp rather than amplifying starlight.

title: Mammography
description: Finds breast cancer early, often before a lump can be felt. The breast is pressed flat between two plastic plates, and low-energy X-rays pass through it onto film or a detector. Tumours and tiny specks of calcium absorb more X-rays than the soft tissue around them, so they show up as white spots.
draw: A mammography machine on its own: an upright column holding an arm with the X-ray tube head at the top, a flat detector plate at chest height below it, and a clear plastic compression paddle lowered close above the plate. No patient.
flag: Gros's Senographe (Strasbourg, 1965-66, built by CGR) was the first dedicated mammography machine; Robert Egan's film technique in Houston (1960-62) is also credited.

title: Quartz watch
description: A watch accurate to a few seconds a month. A tiny quartz crystal rings thousands of times a second: squeezing quartz makes a voltage and a voltage makes it flex, so a battery-powered circuit can keep it ringing. A chip counts the vibrations and gives a little stepping motor one pulse a second to move the hands.
draw: The inside of a quartz wristwatch with the back removed: a round button battery, a small metal cylinder holding the tuning-fork-shaped quartz crystal, a microchip, and the copper coil of the stepping motor beside a train of tiny gears that turns the hands.
flag: Seiko Astron, Tokyo, December 1969; its crystal ran at 8,192 vibrations a second (modern watches use 32,768).

title: Precision-guided bomb
inventor: Texas Instruments and the US Air Force
description: A bomb that steers itself onto its target, landing within a few metres instead of hundreds. A laser beam lights the target with invisible pulses; a sensor in the bomb's nose sees the reflected spot and moves small fins to keep it centred as the bomb glides down. Later kinds steer by satellite navigation instead.
draw: A laser-guided bomb gliding down at a slant against the sky: a plain bomb body with a sensor head on its nose ringed by a short open collar, four small steering fins just behind the nose, and four larger fixed fins at the tail. No markings.
flag: Title made singular. Year changed from 1972 to 1968: Paveway laser-guided bombs were first used in combat in Vietnam in 1968; their famous success, dropping the Thanh Hoa bridge, was 1972. Germany's radio-guided Fritz X (1943) sank a battleship and is an earlier guided bomb.

title: Graphical user interface
description: Lets people use a computer by pointing at pictures instead of typing commands. Every dot on the screen is a bit in the computer's memory, so it can draw overlapping windows, icons and menus; a hand-held mouse moves an arrow across them, and clicking a picture carries out its command.
draw: A desktop computer with an upright, portrait-shaped screen showing overlapping rectangular windows, small icons and an arrow pointer (no readable text), with a keyboard in front and a three-button mouse on the desk beside it, its cable running to the computer.
flag: 1973 is the Xerox Alto, used inside Xerox. Douglas Engelbart showed windows and a mouse in 1968; the Apple Macintosh (1984) brought the idea to the public.

title: Digital camera
description: Takes photographs without film, so pictures can be seen at once and shared by computer. The lens focuses the scene onto an image-sensor chip, where light knocks electrons loose in each of millions of tiny squares; the camera measures the charge in each square and stores the numbers on a memory card.
draw: A compact digital camera cut away from the side: a lens barrel at the front, a flat rectangular sensor chip directly behind the lens, a circuit board behind that, a small memory card half pushed into its slot, and a screen on the back showing the scene in front of the lens.
flag: Sasson's 1975 prototype stored a 0.01-megapixel picture on cassette tape and was never sold; the first cameras people could buy came around 1988-91 (Fuji DS-1P, Dycam, Kodak DCS). Overlaps CCD image sensor (1969).

title: Personal computer
description: A whole computer for one person, on a desk at home or work. At its heart a single microprocessor chip fetches instructions from memory chips and carries them out one after another, from hundreds of thousands to billions of times a second. A keyboard and mouse put information in, a screen shows the results, and a disk keeps files.
draw: A home desk computer: a monitor showing a simple picture, a keyboard and a mouse in front, and a tower case beside it with its side panel off to show the main circuit board, a square processor chip under a finned cooler, slim memory sticks in slots, and a disk drive in a bay.
flag: 1977 is when the Apple II, Commodore PET and TRS-80 went on sale ready-built; the Altair 8800 kit (1975) came first. Overlaps Computers (1930) and Microchips (1975).

title: Portable music player
description: Carries your music with you, played into lightweight headphones as you walk. The first ones played cassettes: a thin plastic tape coated with magnetised particles slides past a playback head, and the changing magnetism makes a tiny current that is amplified for the earphones. Later players store music as numbers in flash memory.
draw: A pocket cassette player with its lid open: the cassette inside, its tape running past a small metal playback head pressed against it, and a steel capstan with a rubber pinch roller squeezing the tape to pull it along. A pair of lightweight headphones on a thin wire plugged into the side.
flag: 1979 is Sony's Walkman. Transistor radios (1954) were portable earlier; digital flash-memory players arrived around 1998.

title: Airbag
description: A cushion that bursts out of the steering wheel in a crash and catches the head before it hits. A sensor feels the sudden slowing and fires a pellet of chemicals that turns, in about a thirtieth of a second, into nitrogen gas filling a nylon bag; vents let the bag deflate as you land on it.
draw: A car's steering wheel with a fully inflated round airbag bursting out of its centre, the torn cover flaps folded open around the hub, and the bag's fabric showing its stitched seams. Empty driver's seat behind, no person.
flag: Year changed from 1981 to 1973: GM sold airbags on some Oldsmobile Toronados in 1973 and as an option on big GM cars in 1974-76; Mercedes-Benz's 1981 S-Class is where they caught on. John Hetrick and Walter Linderer patented the idea in 1951-53.

title: Mobile phone
description: A telephone you carry, so you can call from almost anywhere. The land is divided into small cells, each with its own radio mast; the phone talks to the nearest one and is handed on to the next as you move. Cells far enough apart reuse the same frequencies, so millions of people can call at once.
draw: A hand holding a large brick-shaped handheld phone with a keypad and a stubby rubber antenna on top, raised toward the ear; behind, out of focus, a lattice-steel radio mast with flat panel antennas near its top.
flag: Cooper made the first handheld call in 1973; the DynaTAC went on sale with the first US cell network in 1983. Japan (1979) and Scandinavia (1981) had cellular car-phone networks first.

title: Stealth aircraft
description: A warplane that radar can barely see. Its skin is made of flat, angled panels that bounce radar waves off in a few directions away from the transmitter, like a tilted mirror, instead of back to it; special coatings soak up much of the rest as heat, so even a large jet returns only a faint echo.
draw: A black jet seen from slightly below and ahead, built entirely of flat triangular and trapezoidal panels meeting at sharp angles, with sharply swept wings, a cockpit canopy of flat angled panes, and two tail fins splayed outward in a V. No rounded surfaces.
flag: 1983 is when the F-117 became operational (kept secret until 1988); its demonstrator Have Blue flew in 1977. The shaping rests on equations by Soviet physicist Pyotr Ufimtsev.

title: Flash memory
description: Keeps photos, music and files when the power is off, in phones, cameras and memory sticks. Each bit is a little charge of electrons trapped on an island of conductor sealed in very thin insulation above a transistor. A high voltage pushes electrons through the insulation by quantum tunnelling, and the trapped charge decides whether the transistor switches on.
draw: A memory stick with its plastic casing opened: a small green circuit board carrying a flat black memory chip, a smaller controller chip, and a metal plug connector at one end.
flag: Masuoka invented flash at Toshiba (NOR type shown 1984, NAND 1987); Intel sold the first flash chips in 1988, and Toshiba's NAND reached the market about 1989.

title: Keyhole surgery
description: Operations through cuts a centimetre long instead of opening the body, so patients go home in days rather than weeks. The belly is puffed up with carbon dioxide to make room; a thin telescope lit through glass fibres sends a camera picture to a screen, while the surgeon works with long, slender instruments through other small holes.
draw: An operating table seen from the side: a patient's draped, gently domed belly with three or four slim metal tubes entering it, a surgeon's gloved hands holding long thin instruments through two of them, and a video screen above showing a pink view of the inside.
flag: 1987 is Mouret's video-guided gallbladder removal in Lyon; Erich Mühe (Germany) removed one through a scope in 1985, and Kurt Semm did a keyhole appendectomy in 1980.

title: Lithium-ion battery
inventor: Akira Yoshino, John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham; Sony
description: The light, rechargeable battery in phones, laptops and electric cars. Charging drives lithium ions out of a layered metal-oxide crystal, through a liquid, and slips them between the layers of graphite in the other electrode; using the battery lets them drift back while electrons flow the long way round, through the device.
draw: A cylindrical battery cell cut open lengthwise: inside the steel can, long thin strips (copper foil coated black with graphite, a paper-thin separator, aluminium foil coated with grey metal oxide, another separator) wound together into a tight spiral roll, with the positive cap on top.
flag: Sony sold the first in 1991; Whittingham, Goodenough and Yoshino shared the 2019 Nobel Prize for it. Overlaps Lithium battery (1972).

title: Military drone
description: An aircraft with no one aboard that watches or strikes from far away, flown by a crew on the ground, perhaps on another continent. A camera ball under the nose sends live video up to a satellite and down to the crew, whose commands return the same way; long, thin wings let it circle for a day.
draw: A slender unmanned aircraft in flight, seen from below and to the side: a long thin body with a bulging rounded nose and no cockpit windows, a camera ball hanging under the nose, very long narrow straight wings, an inverted-V tail with its fins pointing downward, and a propeller at the very back pushing it along.
flag: Title made singular. 1995 is the Predator over Bosnia, the first flown by satellite link. Ryan 'Lightning Bug' spy drones flew thousands of missions over Vietnam from 1964, and Israeli drones were used over Lebanon in 1982.

title: Antiretroviral HIV therapy
description: Turns HIV infection from a death sentence into a condition people live with. The virus copies its genes into the cell's DNA with an enzyme called reverse transcriptase, then needs a second enzyme, protease, to finish new viruses; the drugs jam these enzymes. Taking three at once means the virus would need several lucky mutations together to escape.
draw: A weekly pill organiser with its lids open, each day's compartment holding the same trio of pills: one white oval tablet, one blue capsule and one small yellow round tablet.
flag: 1996 is three-drug combination therapy (with the new protease inhibitors), announced at the Vancouver AIDS conference; the first single drug, AZT, came in 1987. Credit is collective; David Ho is the name most often attached.

title: Wireless network
description: Connects laptops, phones and printers to the internet without cables, across a home or office. A router and each device trade short radio bursts at a few billion waves a second. Newer versions split the data across dozens of neighbouring frequencies sent at once, which the receiving chip separates by Fourier analysis, so echoes off walls do not scramble it.
draw: A home wireless router on a wooden shelf: a flat box with three upright antennas and a row of small indicator lights, a laptop open on a table nearby, with faint concentric ripples spreading from the antennas to suggest radio waves.
flag: Title changed from 'Wi-Fi', a trademark. 1997 is the first standard (IEEE 802.11, committee chaired by Vic Hayes of NCR); NCR's WaveLAN (Netherlands, 1991) came before, and home use spread from 1999. The many-frequency method (OFDM) came with 802.11a/g (1999-2003), using a CSIRO (Australia) patent.

title: Ion thruster
description: Pushes a spacecraft for months on end using a tenth of a rocket's fuel. Powered by solar panels, it strips electrons off xenon atoms, and charged metal grids at the back fling the ions out at about 30 kilometres a second. The push is as gentle as a sheet of paper resting on your hand, but never lets up.
draw: The back of a spacecraft with large solar panels: a round thruster whose face is a slightly domed metal grid pierced with thousands of tiny holes, from which a faint glowing blue plume streams straight back into black space.
flag: Re Boris's note: thrust is tiny (Deep Space 1's was under a tenth of a newton) but it uses about ten times less propellant than a chemical rocket, so it wins on long missions. 1998 is Deep Space 1, the first probe driven mainly by one; Kaufman's design first flew on SERT 1 (1964). Ion and related Hall thrusters now drive probes like Dawn and keep thousands of communications satellites in orbit.

title: Short-range wireless link
description: Links earbuds, keyboards, watches and speakers to a phone or computer across a room. Each device sends weak radio signals at 2.4 billion waves a second and hops between 79 channels 1,600 times a second, in a pattern both ends know, so it dodges interference from other gadgets nearby.
draw: A pair of small wireless earbuds lifted out of their open charging case on a table, with a smartphone lying beside them; no wires anywhere.
flag: 1999 is the first Bluetooth specification; Haartsen designed it at Ericsson from 1994, and the first products (headsets) came in 2000.

title: Video calling
description: Lets people talk face to face across the world, seeing each other as they speak. A small camera captures about thirty pictures a second; software squeezes them by sending mostly what changed since the last picture, breaks them into packets and sends them over the internet, where the other computer rebuilds and shows them alongside the sound.
draw: A laptop open on a kitchen table, a small camera lens in the frame above its screen; on the screen a grandmother's face, smiling and waving, while a child sitting in front of the laptop waves back.
flag: Collective. 2003 is when free internet video calls reached ordinary users (Apple's iChat AV with a webcam; Skype launched that year but added video in 2006). AT&T's Picturephone offered video calls over phone lines in 1964-70.

title: Cloud data centre
description: Lets people and companies rent computing power and storage over the internet instead of owning machines. Warehouse-sized buildings hold tens of thousands of computers in racks; software spreads each job and copies each file across many of them, so any one can fail unnoticed. Most of the electricity ends up as heat, which fans and chilled water carry away.
draw: A long, narrow aisle between two rows of tall black server racks, each packed with flat computers stacked like trays, rows of tiny green and blue lights, bundled cables, and perforated floor tiles in front of the racks blowing cool air up into them.
flag: Title made singular. 2006 is when Amazon Web Services began renting storage and computers; Google and others had built warehouse-scale data centres a few years earlier.

title: Electric car
inventor: Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning, Tesla
description: A car that runs on stored electricity instead of petrol, with no exhaust. Thousands of lithium-ion cells under the floor feed electric motors, where currents in copper coils make a rotating magnetic field that drags the rotor round. When the driver brakes, the motor runs as a generator, turning motion back into charge.
draw: Cutaway of a car showing its chassis: a flat battery pack of many cylindrical cells filling the floor between the front and rear wheels, a compact electric motor between the rear wheels joined to them by short drive shafts, and a charging cable plugged into a socket on the side.
flag: Electric cars were common around 1900 (Andreas Flocken, 1888; William Morrison, 1890); 2008 is the Tesla Roadster, the first production car on lithium-ion cells, and the Nissan Leaf (2010) the first mass-market one. Consider titling it 'Modern electric car'.

title: CRISPR gene editing
description: Lets scientists change a chosen spot in the DNA of a living cell, to breed crops or treat inherited disease. A protein called Cas9 carries a short strand of RNA that matches the target; it slides along the DNA until the letters pair up, then cuts both strands. As the cell repairs the cut, the gene is disabled or rewritten.
draw: A molecular-scale view: a large rounded protein clamped around a stretch of DNA double helix; inside it the helix is unzipped, and a short single strand of guide RNA lies paired with one DNA strand, while just beside it both DNA strands are snipped through.
flag: Doudna (Berkeley) and Charpentier (then in Umeå, Sweden) showed the cut in a test tube in 2012; Feng Zhang and George Church used it in human cells in 2013. Nobel Prize 2020.

title: GLP-1 drugs
inventor: John Eng; Amylin and Eli Lilly
description: Medicines that help people with diabetes control their blood sugar, and help many lose weight. They copy a gut hormone released after meals that tells the pancreas to release insulin, slows the stomach, and tells the brain you are full. The body's own hormone is broken down in minutes; the drugs are altered to last a day or a week.
draw: A pen-shaped injector with a dose dial at one end, its cap off and a very short fine needle at the tip, held against the skin of a person's belly.
flag: Year changed from 2017 to 2005: the first GLP-1 drug, exenatide (from Gila monster saliva, found by John Eng), was approved in 2005; 2017 is semaglutide (Novo Nordisk, Denmark) for diabetes and 2021 its approval for weight loss. Hormone research credited to Joel Habener, Svetlana Mojsov, Daniel Drucker and Jens Juul Holst.

title: mRNA vaccines
inventor: Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman; BioNTech, Moderna
description: Teaches the immune system to recognise a virus without meeting it. The injection carries genetic instructions for one virus protein, wrapped in tiny bubbles of fat; muscle cells read the instructions and make the protein, which the immune system learns to attack. The instructions fall apart within days, and the vaccine can be redesigned for a new virus in weeks.
draw: A molecular-scale view at the edge of a cell: a tiny sphere made of fat molecules, partly merged with the cell's outer membrane, releasing coiled single strands of mRNA inside; nearby a ribosome threads along one strand, and spike-shaped proteins stand out on the cell's surface.
